item.title: Catholic Leaders Say Meeting With Trump Wasn’t Intended to Be Political
item.description:
The video, not even 30 seconds long, showed several Roman Catholic bishops praying with President Trump last week in the Oval Office.

That footage, shared on social media by a White House official during the thick of election season, blazed across the internet and became entangled in the fractured politics of the country and the church.

Archbishop James R. Golka of Denver, who led the prayer, told a local Catholic publication that it “was never my intention” for the meeting to be seen as an endorsement.

One attendee, Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, wrote afterward that “I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes.”

Another, Archbishop Jeffrey S. Grob of Milwaukee, publicly apologized on Sunday and claimed that the video had been shared by the White House without the bishops’ permission.

“I feel a heavy sadness, not only over the pain I caused, but also for the fact that something so sacred to a group of religious leaders, prayer to our Heavenly Father, would be manipulated in that way,” Archbishop Grob wrote in an open letter. He added: “We should never have been put in that position by the White House.”

White House officials did not directly comment on Archbishop Grob’s claim that the video was shared without permission.

“There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it,” Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement when asked about the meeting. She said that the president had pardoned anti-abortion activists, “proudly defended and expanded our religious rights” and “stopped the weaponization of the federal government against Christians.”

The prayer itself — at least the snippet of it shared by the White House — was not explicitly political.

Archbishop Golka, with his hand on Mr. Trump’s shoulder, said, “Thank you for the gift of our great beautiful nation; thank you for the gift of our government; thank you for the gift of this office of presidency. We lift up our president and ask your blessing upon him.”

The video, posted on X by the White House official Margo Martin, appeared to start mid-prayer and seemed to end before the archbishop had finished. Footage of the meeting was also posted on a Facebook page for Mr. Trump’s political operation with the caption, “FAITH FRIDAYS: This White House prays together.”

American Catholics are politically mixed.

Pew Research Center data from 2023 found that about 52 percent of Catholics were Republicans or leaned Republican, and 44 percent were Democrats or leaned toward Democrats. Former President Joseph R. Biden Jr., a Democrat, and Vice President JD Vance, a Republican, are both Catholic.

Catholic leaders have historically called out presidential administrations of both parties for actions seen as contrary to the church’s teachings. Mr. Biden was often criticized for his support for abortion rights. And Pope Leo XIV, the first American pontiff, has often been publicly at odds with Mr. Trump.

Last year, Archbishop Grob and other Wisconsin bishops signed a letter voicing “strong concern regarding the indiscriminate nature of the current federal immigration enforcement.”

In his apology on Sunday, Archbishop Grob said he had been joined by 11 other bishops at the White House in a meeting organized by the Heritage Foundation, a conservative group.

Archbishop Grob said he had been “told the meeting was to be a private discussion, that several Catholic members of the cabinet might make an appearance, and that there could be an opportunity to pray privately with the president.” He said he had not intended to endorse “the president, his policies or his party.”

“We came in good faith to try to work for the betterment of our fellow human beings, to ease their suffering, to build up the common good and to pray with a president, not to pose for a political photo opportunity to benefit the few,” Archbishop Grob wrote.

Bishop Joensen of Des Moines wrote that “there are many things tied to this present administration that are blatantly at odds with our Catholic faith,” but that he often engages with officials who hold differing views.

“None of us bishops were unaware that our meeting was on the cusp of a national election,” Bishop Joensen wrote. “Yet in no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate. That said, in retrospect, I would have done well to be more mindful of Jesus’ admonition: ‘Behold, I am sending you like sheep in the midst of wolves; so be shrewd as serpents and simple as doves.’”

In an interview with Denver Catholic, an archdiocese publication, Archbishop Golka described praying about the invitation.

“Though I originally thought it would be a private meeting, I knew that it could be shared and that some might use it for political purposes,” the archbishop said. “But as I prayed about it, I thought that this is what Catholics do. We pray for people. No matter whether we agree or disagree on anything, we always pray for our country and leaders.”

item.title: How Obama and Trump Made Their Cases in Dueling Midterm Speeches
item.description:
Former President Barack Obama returned to the campaign trail on Saturday for midterm rallies in Cleveland and Detroit, setting up a rare split screen with President Trump, who staged a rally in the evening in a small city in central Georgia.

Their pitches offered a contrast in style and substance. Mr. Obama prosecuted his case against the Trump administration in two tightly scripted, roughly 40-minute bursts on Saturday.

Mr. Trump, who has been crisscrossing the country for weeks in a midterm push to save his party’s congressional majorities, defended his administration in a rambling and at times profane hour-and-a-half speech Saturday night.

Here’s how Mr. Trump and Mr. Obama made their arguments 10 days before the election.

Mr. Obama assailed the Iran war, which has driven up prices, describing it as an “unnecessary war” that “nobody asked for.”

“Our allies and our bases have been attacked,” Mr. Obama said in Cleveland. “Americans have been killed. Hundreds of Americans have been wounded. We have run down our stock of missiles. And Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil goes through to the world market.”

He said a central goal of the war — preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon — had been better addressed through the nuclear deal he reached with Iran in 2015. Mr. Trump pulled out of that agreement during his first term.

Mr. Trump said the unpopular war had been a success and had cowed Iran. He said Mr. Obama’s deal had been a “road to a nuclear weapon for Iran.”

“We defeated them militarily, financially and otherwise,” Mr. Trump said of Iran, though the war continues and administration officials are concerned that Iran is in the advanced stages of plans for attacks against U.S. officials.

“We have to make sure that they never, ever have a nuclear weapon, and we’ll do that very easily,” Mr. Trump said, adding, “Our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time.”

Mr. Trump spent much of his speech warning about a risk he said Democrats would pose to the economy. A vote for Republicans, Mr. Trump said, was a vote for “more money in your pockets,” lower taxes and a “booming” economy.

If the Democrats win back Congress, he claimed, the country will fall into a “1929-style economic depression the likes of which you have never seen before.”

“They want all the things financially bad,” Mr. Trump said, citing transgender athletes in women’s sports, without explaining how that could affect the economy.

Mr. Trump also reminded voters of his promise to send $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans win in November. He argued that his sweeping tariff policies had “made us rich” and led to companies “pouring in” to the United States.

Mr. Obama said that presidents did not have “control over the entire economy.” But in this case the “administration’s actions are directly responsible for rising costs,” he said, citing the Iran war.

“This is the reason why the price of oil is up — nobody disputes that,” Mr. Obama said. “This is the reason the price of diesel is up. This is the reason why the price of just about everything is up.”

Mr. Obama ridiculed Mr. Trump’s tariff regimen, saying it, too, had contributed to rising prices. He mocked Mr. Trump for picking a trade fight with “that well-known evil empire Canada.” And he suggested that Republicans should have passed legislation responding to inflation.

“The only bill they passed of any significance in the last two years was a trillion-dollar tax break that mostly benefited the richest Americans,” Mr. Obama said.

Mr. Obama pushed back on a core Republican argument going into November: that Democratic candidates are extreme.

Mr. Obama, chuckling, said in Detroit that Republicans’ ads were aimed at convincing voters that his party was made up of “radicals or communists or jihadists or the woke police that will come arrest you and force-feed you tofu.”

“We are not going to fall for that okey-doke,” Mr. Obama said.

Mr. Obama was joining Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, who is in a close race and whose platform calls for universal health care. Mr. Obama objected to Republican efforts to cast Dr. El-Sayed as extreme.

“Wanting everybody to have health care — how is that radical?” Mr. Obama said. “Wanting everybody to have a place to live that they can afford — how is that radical?”

Around the same time, Mr. Trump was arguing in Perry, Ga., that his party was running against “radical-left” candidates. He claimed that Democrats wanted to “loot your wealth” and “annihilate your borders.”

He charged that Democrats were running as communists, though no Democrat in any midterm race of note identifies as a communist. (Some Democratic candidates, mostly concentrated in deep-blue districts, identify as democratic socialists.)

“Less than two years ago, the radical-left Democrats handed us the dark age — it was a dark age — of America,” Mr. Trump said in Georgia, where he described the incumbent Democratic senator on the ballot, Jon Ossoff, as a “radical-left senator.”

Mr. Ossoff, a mainstream Democrat, has held a durable lead in the polls over his Republican challenger, Representative Mike Collins.

Mr. Trump and Mr. Obama offered different takes on the most pressing issues facing the country.

Mr. Trump said the “hardest job” was addressing the threat posed by immigration. He cast economic challenges as comparatively minor, and said deporting immigrants was “nasty work.”

“Some of them are so dangerous, Rick, we don’t want to get them out, we have to put them in jail,” Mr. Trump said, speaking from the stage to Rick Jackson, the Republican nominee for Georgia governor.

Mr. Obama said in Detroit that “we do need to make sure our border is orderly and secure,” but suggested that Mr. Trump had reached beyond his 2024 campaign promises by “sending masked agents running through our streets.”

And he questioned whether Mr. Trump was “thinking deeply” about the challenges facing Americans. As he closed his speech, he reflected on artificial intelligence.

“I know it’s been hyped, but there is a real technology that’s coming,” Mr. Obama said. “It is going to change a lot.”

He added: “These are serious times. This is not the time for reality TV.”

(Both presidents are set to return to the trail before the Nov. 3 election.)

item.title: In Islamophobic Rant, Trump Seeks to Stir Republican Base in Michigan
item.description:
President Trump turned to Islamophobic stereotypes to motivate Michigan Republicans on Sunday, claiming at a rally that Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee, if elected, would bring a wave of jihadists to the United States.

“If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas,” Mr. Trump told more than 4,000 supporters gathered in Port Huron, a working-class, waterfront city in a deep-red congressional district 60 miles northeast of Detroit.

Mr. Trump called Dr. El-Sayed, whose family immigrated from Egypt, a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member,” a baseless claim. He then contrasted Dr. El-Sayed, a Muslim who was born in the United States, with his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, who is white and also born in the United States.

“I call him apple pie,” Mr. Trump said of Mr. Rogers, who is 63. “He’s like, perfect, this guy. He’s like central casting. He’s what your state is all about.”

Mr. Trump’s comments, coming in a key midterm battleground nine days before the elections, underscored the dark themes and personal vilification he and his allies have embraced as part of their closing pitch. And while he has often used crude and racist language, Mr. Trump’s message in Michigan seemed aimed at overtly stoking a fear of Muslims to get voters to the polls.

But a broader question about Mr. Trump’s rally here — which followed several in North and South Carolina, Georgia and Florida, among other stops — is whether his presence helps or hurts Republican turnout in a year when polls show deep dissatisfaction with the president. His audience in Port Huron seemed enthusiastic, and thousands strained to take Mr. Trump’s picture as he took to the stage. But he held the rally in a conservative district of a state that pollsters believe is swinging back to Democrats.

Mr. Trump’s deep unpopularity has complicated Republicans’ path to victory. While Mr. Trump carried Michigan by two points in 2024, just 34 percent of likely voters now approve of him, according to a New York Times/Siena poll conducted in mid-September.

Polls indicate that Dr. El-Sayed, 41, has a narrow edge over Mr. Rogers in a race that will be pivotal to determining control of the Senate.

Mr. Trump’s attacks on Dr. El-Sayed on Sunday, questioning his loyalty to the United States, began before he got on Air Force One outside of Washington and accelerated after he landed in Michigan.

Speaking in a town on the Canadian border, Mr. Trump did not dwell on his battle with Prime Minister Mark Carney, one of the few world leaders who has directly confronted him on tariffs and other issues, and he did not repeat his frequent call for Canada to give up its independence and become the 51st state.

Instead, he focused on Dr. El-Sayed, his religion and his relatives. Mr. Trump also disparaged Jewish voters who were considering voting for Dr. El-Sayed.

“Any Jewish person that supports this guy should be ashamed of themselves,” Mr. Trump said, adding that he “cannot understand how anybody who’s Jewish can even think about voting for this guy.”

Hundreds of Jewish voters in Michigan publicly announced they were backing Dr. El-Sayed, while others have said they are voting for Mr. Rogers or threatened to withhold their support.

Mr. Trump made the statement after claiming that Dr. El-Sayed’s half sister, Eman Abdelhadi, celebrated the Oct. 7, 2023, massacre of Israelis by Hamas fighters.

She posted a video on the first anniversary of the attack that said that “no matter how great the brutality, the oppression, the intensity of what we’re going through, the horizon of justice is just around the corner,” but did not mention the massacre directly and did not celebrate the violence. Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign told Fox News that he disagreed with her “on a number of political positions and the rhetoric she’s chosen to use.”

Dr. El-Sayed has repeatedly disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist political movement, and has said comments about his name and faith are attempts to distract from voters’ economic woes. His aides have said claims of ties to overseas terrorist groups are racist and Islamophobic.

But his opponents have raised an open letter he signed in 2012, when he was a medical student. It was addressed to Mohamed Morsi, then the new Egyptian president, from a party that represents the political wing of the Muslim Brotherhood. It asked him to “purge the media and police” of loyalists to the government that was overturned during the Arab Spring.

Dr. El-Sayed has not discussed the letter. But his spokesman, Cole Wozniak, said, “Abdul remains laser-focused on his plans to bring down costs and stand up to the chaos and corruption in Washington.”

“Michigan knows Trump is on the ballot on Nov. 3,” he added, “and they will vote like it by rejecting Trump’s rubber stamp Mike Rogers and sending Abdul to the Senate.”

Mr. Trump deepened his critique as the day went on, saying that someone with Dr. El-Sayed’s background “would be screened and unable to get a seat on an airplane. They certainly should not give him a seat in the United States Senate.” He also said that Dr. El-Sayed should not be given access to classified information.

At his own rally on Sunday in Grand Rapids, Dr. El-Sayed said the Republican strategy was “to point at me and my name and my faith. But my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your gas.”In Michigan, Mr. Trump also veered into a discussion of Greenland. He insisted, “Oh, you know we did get Greenland,” suggesting that it was now owned by the United States. In fact, Mr. Trump was forced to drop that demand and instead signed a new treaty with Denmark, which handles Greenland’s foreign affairs, that envisions opening two new U.S. bases on the island and bars similar arrangements with foreign powers, notably China. But it does not change Denmark’s sovereignty, as Mr. Trump initially insisted.

He also drew cheers when he insisted Iran would never get a nuclear weapon, and vaguely said the war with Iran would be resolved soon. But he largely steered clear of discussing how his decision to attack Iran led directly to high gas and diesel prices.

Mr. Rogers has sought distance from the war, calling for it to “end quickly,” and from the president’s tariffs on Canadian goods, saying “Canada is not our enemy” in a campaign ad. He has also backed a one-year moratorium on data centers, creating a contrast with Mr. Trump’s support for them.

Like other Republicans, Mr. Rogers has largely avoided talking about Mr. Trump in ads and on the campaign trail.

Speaking at the rally in Port Huron, Mr. Rogers again accused Dr. El-Sayed of having family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. He said that watching Dr. El-Sayed try to tell the truth is like “watching an octopus put his socks on in the morning.” And he said the country “can’t risk his extreme ideology and thinking.”

On NBC News’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday morning, Mr. Rogers did not endorse Mr. Trump’s baseless claim that Dr. El-Sayed is “a terrorist,” but did not condemn it outright.

“I’ve never called him a terrorist,” Mr. Rogers said of Dr. El-Sayed.

Dr. El-Sayed has become a central villain in Republicans’ narrative of the midterms. In Western Iowa on Thursday, more than 800 miles from Port Huron, Mr. Trump railed against Dr. El- Sayed, drawing some of the loudest applause of the night. He did the same in North Carolina and Ohio earlier this week.

After holding forth on the potential demise of the nation in Michigan on Sunday, Mr. Trump spent five full minutes admiring the body and physicality of Senator Jon Husted, the Republican running for re-election in Ohio, and the rapper Nicki Minaj, who traveled with Mr. Trump to the rally.

“I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before — Nicki Minaj,” Mr. Trump said. “Hard to miss it.”

]]>

item.description: When Hurricane Helene hit western North Carolina in 2024, hundreds of households lost the private bridges they rely on to access their homes. Two years later, only 44 bridges have been rebuilt by the state. Our reporter Eduardo Medina takes us there. ]]>

item.title: The 11 Midterm Races That Could Shape the Progressive Movement’s Future
item.description:
California’s conservative Central Valley is not where you’d expect Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont progressive, to hold a campaign rally ahead of the midterms.

But this working-class region of grape farmers and cattle ranchers, parched by 100-degree autumn heat, was Mr. Sanders’s destination one recent October evening as he strove to usher in the wave of left-wing populism that he has dreamed of for decades.

The left’s incursion this year into Republican turf, far from the liberal cities that have long served as its base of support, shows either how many gains progressives have made this election season or how wrong they are about what everyday Americans think of left-wing politics.

The answer will arrive on Nov. 3.

All year, Mr. Sanders and his allies have promised that their liberal candidates, backing ambitious goals including taxing billionaires and passing “Medicare for all,” would prove more popular with voters than centrist Democrats and their more cautious rhetoric. Left-wing candidates embracing such policies scored a raft of wins in Democratic primaries, not only in deep-blue cities but also in competitive races where Democrats have traditionally picked moderates to face Republican opponents.

But the left has insisted that its working-class focus and bold agenda are resonating even among moderates and Republicans in the general election, and in battleground districts such as the Central Valley. It’s a bet with potentially huge consequences, given how crucial these districts are to Democrats’ hopes of winning control of Congress.

If progressive candidates win big, they will most likely claim a mandate from the electorate to push left-wing policies in Congress next year. Failure, however, would allow the Democratic establishment to continue to argue that moderate and independent voters prefer centrist politicians — which will inform which types of candidates the party will encourage as it seeks to expand the map of places it can compete in. And midterm losses would also most likely set back progressives seeking to play a role in the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028.

Aware of the stakes, Mr. Sanders has embarked on a final-stretch campaign swing across the country to shore up his progressive protégés. In the Central Valley, he rallied in Bakersfield in support of Randy Villegas, the left-wing challenger to Representative David Valadao, a tenacious Republican who has resisted past challengers but has been made newly vulnerable by redistricting.

In an interview there, Mr. Sanders said he was focused primarily on campaigning for progressive Democrats in four competitive Senate races: Michigan, Maine, Minnesota and Florida. He said Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota faces “a tougher race than some people think,” while in Florida, he believed Angie Nixon could pull off an upset victory, “and I would not be shocked if she won.”

“I am doing everything I can to see that Democrats regain control of the House and the Senate,” Mr. Sanders said.

Self-described progressive or populist candidates are running for office all over the map. We examined roughly a dozen races that are being closely watched as tests of the viability of the progressive movement. Here is a look at how the left-leaning candidates could perform on Election Day, based on the current ratings of each of these races by The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan prognosticator.

In several races, progressive candidates with strong polling numbers are running in districts that currently tilt toward Democrats. They are considered slight favorites to defeat their Republican opponents.

Peggy Flanagan, the lieutenant governor in Minnesota, is running for the U.S. Senate. She is favored in a state that Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024 by four percentage points, but she has been dragged down by a major fraud scandal. Michele Tafoya, her Republican opponent and a former N.F.L. broadcaster, has worked to portray herself as a moderate, in contrast with Ms. Flanagan’s vocal support for Medicare for all and other left-wing positions.

Bob Brooks, a retired firefighter and union leader, is considered a slight favorite in his bid for Pennsylvania’s Seventh District. A progressive who attracted early endorsements from across the political spectrum, including Mr. Sanders and Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, Mr. Brooks faces Representative Ryan Mackenzie, a Republican, in a battleground district in the Lehigh Valley.

Manny Rutinel, a former state legislator in Colorado, is trying to oust Representative Gabe Evans, a Republican, in Colorado’s Eighth District, a suburban area north of Denver. Mr. Evans is considered vulnerable, but Mr. Rutinel, after beating a moderate Democrat in the primary, has faced attacks for his left-wing background. A former animal-rights activist, he has more recently distanced himself from past comments criticizing the consumption of meat and dairy products. He even ate a carne asada taco in front of reporters to prove his change of heart.

Some progressive candidates are running in races that are considered true tossups.

Randy Villegas is no “Valleycrat” — the kind of moderate-to-conservative Central Valley Democrat the party typically runs in California’s 22nd District. Mr. Villegas defeated a moderate in the primary, and has spoken openly about his alliance with Mr. Sanders and his desire for Medicare for all. He is betting that his populist policies will resonate in one of California’s more impoverished regions, while Republicans are trying to paint him as far too liberal. Last year’s Democratic redrawing of the district could help push Mr. Villegas over the finish line against Mr. Valadao, the Republican incumbent.

Sam Forstag, a former labor leader and smokejumper — a specialized type of firefighter — is trying to flip Montana’s First District, an open seat in the western part of the state. He embraced his progressive roots in the primary, often mentioning in his speeches that he appeared at a rally for Mr. Sanders and campaigning with Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. For the general election in a ruby-red state, Mr. Forstag has scrubbed his website of those endorsements as he faces Aaron Flint, an Army veteran and conservative radio show host.

William Lawrence, a co-founder of the progressive Sunrise Movement, angered the Democratic establishment with some of his past comments, and there was skepticism over whether the party would boost his candidacy in Michigan’s Seventh District after he toppled two centrist candidates in the primary. But Democrats are indeed spending on his behalf as Mr. Lawrence tries to oust Representative Tom Barrett, a Republican.

Troy Jackson, the former president of Maine’s State Senate, replaced Graham Platner — another progressive — on the ballot for the U.S. Senate in Maine in July. Senator Susan Collins, his Republican opponent, is a formidable incumbent. She’s also a moderate running against a populist candidate who has the backing of Mr. Sanders, a contrast Republicans have highlighted as they strain to hold on to the seat in a heavily Democratic state.

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a former county health director, is perhaps the highest-profile progressive on this list, and his success or failure may be viewed as a proxy for the broader movement. Dr. El-Sayed, running for the U.S. Senate in Michigan, overcame tens of millions of dollars in outside spending during a primary that pitted him against a moderate opponent. Now, centrist Democrats are terrified that his left-wing views — he is a vocal critic of Israel — could help Mike Rogers, his Republican opponent, and cost the party a crucial seat. Progressives including Mr. Sanders and Ms. Ocasio-Cortez have campaigned with him.

Some progressive candidates are running in redder areas, and Republicans are currently favored in those races.

Matt Dunlap, the Maine state auditor and former Maine secretary of state, is backed by Our Revolution, the left-wing organization founded by alumni of Mr. Sanders’s campaigns. He’s trying to maintain Democratic control of Maine’s Second District, a rural region currently represented by Representative Jared Golden, a far more moderate politician who is retiring and seems like a more natural fit with the district. Analysts have given Mr. Dunlap’s Republican opponent, former Gov. Paul LePage, the edge.

Angie Nixon is running for the U.S. Senate in Florida, a state President Trump won by 13 points in 2024. A member of the Democratic Socialists of America, Ms. Nixon shocked her party’s establishment with an upset win in the primary, and some prognosticators think there’s a chance she could do the same against Senator Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent, in November. Mr. Sanders and Ms. Ocasio-Cortez have campaigned for her, too, but Ms. Moody remains heavily favored.

Justin Pearson, a state lawmaker in Tennessee, rose to political fame when he was briefly expelled from the State Legislature in 2023 after participating in a gun control protest on the House floor. With the support of progressive groups like Justice Democrats, he mounted a challenge to Representative Steve Cohen, a Democrat, in a safely Democratic seat in Memphis. But a Republican-led redistricting effort redrew Tennessee’s Ninth District into one that is considered a safe Republican pickup and prompted Mr. Cohen to announce his retirement. Despite Mr. Pearson’s underdog status against Brent Taylor, a Republican state legislator, Democrats are bullish on their candidate’s chances, and Ms. Ocasio-Cortez has campaigned with him.

Taylor Robinson contributed reporting.

item.title: Democratic Attorneys General Have Defied Trump. Some May Fall on Nov. 3.
item.description:
Democratic attorneys general have operated for two years as the tip of the spear in their party’s confrontations with President Trump, suing him 100 times on issues ranging from the deployment of National Guard troops to tariffs and the withholding of federal funds.

But a week before Election Day, it remains unclear whether midterm voters will fortify that front by electing Democratic attorneys general in Kansas and Iowa, or take down two of its members, Keith Ellison of Minnesota and Kris Mayes of Arizona.

In a midterm cycle where Democrats appear poised to make significant gains in Congress, governorships and statehouses, the races for attorney general are murkier. Often they hinge on localized concerns like crime and public safety that can favor Republicans. Sometimes they can also be caught up in a nationalized political environment.

For Republicans, national worries loom large in states such as Iowa and Georgia. Adam Piper, executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association, warned in a memo last month, “Current alarms are not smoke detectors beeping from burnt popcorn, but indicators of fires in states that Republicans have taken for granted for decades.”

The biggest G.O.P. worry is in Kansas, where the incumbent attorney general, Kris Kobach, a longtime conservative fixture and sometime lightning rod, faces a rematch against Chris Mann, a former police officer and prosecutor. Mr. Kobach has cautioned that his race could be affected by the U.S. Senate contest, in which Democrats have been energized by Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, against the incumbent, Senator Roger Marshall.

For Democrats, the headache is in Minnesota, where the attorney general, Keith Ellison, is fighting for his political life. At a rally this month in Rochester, Minn., Zack Filipovich, the Democratic candidate for state auditor, pleaded Mr. Ellison’s case for him.

“Our attorney general is here to protect all of us from everything coming at us from the White House, from the Trump administration, and by his cronies in Congress,” Mr. Filipovich said, as Mr. Ellison stood nearby.

Of 30 states electing attorneys general on Nov. 3, eight are considered competitive by campaign strategists and MultiState, a government relations firm tracking statehouse races. Out of those states, which include battlegrounds like Wisconsin, Georgia and Nevada, five currently have Democratic attorneys general, and three have Republicans.

Republicans believe they can flip Michigan, where a high-profile U.S. Senate race and control of the State Legislature are also at stake. Two county prosecutors are vying to succeed Dana Nessel: Eli Savit, a progressive Democrat and former clerk to the Supreme Court justices Sandra Day O’Connor and Ruth Bader Ginsburg; and Doug Lloyd, a Republican prosecutor with three decades of experience.

In Florida, the Republican attorney general, James Uthmeier, who was tapped by Gov. Ron DeSantis in February to replace Ashley Moody when she was appointed to the U.S. Senate, is facing José Javier Rodríguez, a former state legislator and assistant labor secretary in the Biden administration. Buoyed by a late $5 million injection from the Democratic Attorneys General Association, Democrats have hammered Mr. Uthmeier for his connection to the DeSantis administration’s steering of $10 million in legal settlement money to a charity linked to the governor’s wife.

In Arizona, Ms. Mayes — who won by just 280 votes in 2022 — faces Warren Petersen, the State Senate president, who has repeatedly questioned the 2020 presidential election results.

But Minnesota is the marquee matchup.

The state has been a focus of the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement efforts, but has also been reeling from a social services fraud scandal that prompted Gov. Tim Walz, a Democrat, to forgo a third term. Though crime rates have fallen, Republicans have seized on public safety anxieties after recent gang-related suburban shootings.

No Republican has won statewide office since Tim Pawlenty was re-elected governor in 2006, and Mr. Trump remains deeply unpopular. Yet approval ratings are also sagging for many Democrats, including Mr. Ellison, a polarizing progressive and former congressman seeking a third term.

Hoping to unseat him is Ron Schutz, a longtime trial lawyer and Republican activist backed by at least $6.8 million flowing in to defeat Mr. Ellison.

The Schutz campaign did not respond to requests for comment. In debates, however, Mr. Schutz has slammed Mr. Ellison over the fraud scandal; Minnesota, known for its 10,000 lakes, is now “the land of 10,000 frauds,” he said. He also criticized Mr. Ellison’s role in pardoning a Laotian immigrant convicted of child sexual abuse who was subsequently deported by federal immigration authorities.

Mr. Schutz sidestepped questions regarding his views on state lawsuits against the Trump administration. He did agree with Mr. Ellison, however, that the federal government should not have blocked local authorities from investigating the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

In an interview, Mr. Ellison defended his record, stressing his consumer protection efforts to bring down costs, such as a settlement with drug manufacturers to cap insulin prices and one with tribal businesses to stop predatory lending.

Of the 75 multistate lawsuits Minnesota has joined, the most galling, he said, was the Trump administration’s attempt to withhold food stamps during last year’s government shutdown.

“You’ve got to have somebody who will say, ‘The 10th Amendment means that states have some sovereignty,’” he said. “The federal government can’t just roll over us and take our money whenever they feel like it.”

In crucial Twin Cities suburbs like Eden Prairie in Hennepin County and Shakopee in Scott County, some voters viewed the race as a referendum on Mr. Trump. Others saw it as a vote on combating fraud.

Outside the Eden Prairie library, Julimar Castro, 40, said the fraud scandal had been “blown out of proportion” and the Republican Party was being “overtaken by bullies.”

“I usually don’t vote by party, but this year I am,” said Ms. Castro, a mental health professional. “All Democrats.”

In Shakopee, Roxanne Atwood, a 68-year-old retired schoolteacher and a Republican, said she had a history of splitting her ticket. Unlike most people interviewed, she was familiar with Mr. Schutz, calling him “a little too conservative.”

Yet despite voting previously for Mr. Ellison, she said she could not do so again.

“I believe that he was involved in the fraud,” she said. “I think he and Governor Walz knew what was going on, and they just didn’t want to take the time to deal with it. You have to pay attention — you have to pay attention to what’s happening in our state, what’s happening with our finances.”

item.title: In Fight for the Senate, Democrats Face a Once-in-a-Generation Test
item.description:
Senator Roger Marshall, the first-term Republican incumbent, is under siege in Kansas with the midterms just days off. Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate in Texas and the state’s attorney general, is embroiled in multiple unsavory scandals and struggling.

Polls also show Democratic Senate candidates running strong in Iowa and Alaska, and on the cusp of victory in North Carolina, playing offense in what should be safe Republican terrain. At the same time, independent candidates are within striking distance of Republican Senate candidates in Montana, Nebraska and even South Dakota.

“This is as good a political environment as Democrats could ever wish,” said Amy Walter, the editor of the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, “and as bad as Republicans could ever imagine.”

Yet with the exception of North Carolina, it is far from certain that Democrats can pull off a single upset in any of the red states typically considered out of reach for them. They are competing not only against individual Republicans but also against ideological and structural advantages that have turned those states into reliable G.O.P. strongholds and locked down the Senate map in recent years.

It wasn’t long ago that Nebraska, Montana, Iowa, the Dakotas and Alaska were represented by Democratic senators. But Republicans have solidified their grip on those states, suggesting that if Democrats cannot make inroads in this election, when Republicans are on the ropes, it could be some time before they again have such an opening.

“If you can’t win under these conditions, you ain’t gonna win for a long time,” said Jon Tester, the former Democratic senator from Montana who lost his seat in 2024 after three terms as his state moved away from Democrats. He pointed to anti-Trump fervor, soaring fuel costs and the economic struggles of everyday Americans as reasons Republicans were highly vulnerable on their home turf.

The Senate map is always evolving, with population shifts and social conditions sparking changes in party thinking about where to devote attention and resources. As recently as the 1990s, the South was the epicenter of new Democratic thinking, as President Bill Clinton showed that Democrats could still appeal to rural and lower-income voters, and he had plenty of allies from the region on Capitol Hill.

At the time, states like Louisiana and Arkansas were represented by at least one and often two Democratic senators. Conversely, Republicans could still be elected in places like New York, Illinois and the Pacific Northwest.

But that political environment steadily eroded, and Republicans rose in the South and the Great Plains while elected Democrats mostly disappeared there. Pushed out of spots like North Dakota and vast expanses of Middle America, Democrats concentrated on urban areas, promoting a more progressive brand of politics.

That was a big mistake, critics say.

“The national Democratic Party hasn’t done what it should in places like Montana,” said Seth Bodnar, an Army veteran and former president of the University of Montana, who is running as an independent candidate in that state. “This strategy of trading blue-collar workers in rural areas to win in the cities and suburbs — that’s not a strategy for success in Montana.”

Over the years, changes in the map have had a profound effect on the way the parties treat elections, with some states essentially considered the property of one party or another, limiting the battlefield. The number of seats considered truly competitive has dwindled significantly, a phenomenon that started in the House but has taken hold more recently in the Senate.

That has had a major impact on the way the Senate operates, as senators have increasingly retreated to their partisan corners, unconcerned about a threat from across the aisle. In a growing number of states, they need to worry only about primaries, in which the incentive is to move right in the case of Republicans and left for Democrats, which has yielded a profoundly polarized Senate.

At present, just three states — Maine, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin — have split Senate delegations, illustrating how rigid the one-party hold is on Senate seats. It is the lowest total since the direct election of senators began more than a century ago.

But Democrats spied red-state openings this year amid the backlash to Trump administration policies, including tariffs and the war with Iran, which have contributed to high costs and economic pain in parts of the nation that might not otherwise seriously entertain a Democratic candidate. And they have had strong candidates step up.

The contested Senate map has steadily expanded into red states. In recent days, the super PAC aligned with Senator Chuck Schumer, the New York Democrat and minority leader, put more than $1 million into advertising in Mississippi, a state that has not elected a Democratic senator since 1982. But Democrats believe Scott Colom, a state prosecutor, has a chance against the Republican senator, Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Mr. Schumer, who plays a major role in crafting his party’s Senate strategy, dismissed the idea that a failure to cash in on some of the red states this time would mean they would remain out of reach for a stretch.

“I’ll never say never,” Mr. Schumer said. But he acknowledged that this year presented a “unique opportunity.”

“We have so many opportunities in reddish states,” he said. “Two years ago, they would have said this is the most impossible map. Who would have thought Alaska? Who would have thought Kansas? Who would have thought Iowa?”

Just how far Democrats can reach into red America won’t be known until after Election Day, but party strategists say that any wins could position the party for future gains.

“Every once in a while, the bottom falls out for the party in power, and when that happens, it’s possible to dramatically expand the number of states that you can win,” said Adam Jentleson, a former top Democratic Senate aide. He is also the founder of the Searchlight Institute, which aims to expand the Senate battleground and build an enduring Democratic majority.

Mr. Jentleson noted that most senators elected next month will serve through the entirety of the next president’s first term. And history shows that incumbent senators, with all the advantages of office, tend to get re-elected.

With Democrats also poised to win some red-state governorships, Mr. Jentleson said those governors could work with new Democratic senators to restore the party’s presence in states where it has been written off, providing a foundation to build on in coming elections.

He pointed to Republican-held seats in states like Wisconsin and North Carolina that could then be vulnerable in the next election. He said this year’s election could prove similar to 2006, when Democrats seized House and Senate majorities in Congress and then expanded those gains in 2008.

“What this should be for us is 2006 and 2008, when one good cycle leads to another,” Mr. Jentleson said.

But Democrats first have to win next month in states where they have had little success — and that is no sure thing. It presents a test of their possible appeal in states that seemed all but lost to the party.

“If you can’t win now,” said Mr. Tester, the former Democratic senator, “when can you win?”

item.description:
Eight days before the midterm elections, the jitters have taken root.

Political forecasters and strategists are increasingly confident that Democrats will win control of the House next week. But what is remarkable about the Senate is that, so close to Election Day, the battleground map is still wide and unsettled, making both parties nervous.

The spending reflects the ongoing Senate fight: Republicans are outspending Democrats on advertising in the seven Senate races considered tossups by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report. By comparison, Republicans have only a narrow spending edge in House races.

Several scenarios remain possible. Competitive Senate races could tighten in Republicans’ favor as they get their most loyal supporters to the polls. Democrats could do well in red states but struggle in some bluer ones. Or the bottom could fall out for Republicans in a potential wave that Democrats are too apprehensive to consider after past disappointments.

Democrats’ House prospects are so bright that the Cook Political Report has rated a majority of the chamber as leaning Democratic for the first time this election cycle. The report shifted 19 more House races toward Democrats on Friday, meaning that even if Republicans won all 17 races rated as tossups, they would still lose control of the House.

Four of the shifts from “tossup” to “lean Democrat” came in races with Republican incumbents. The report shifted four races in Texas and three in North Carolina because the Republican candidates at the top of the ticket (read: running for Senate) in those states are underperforming.

Last-minute campaign finance activity is a doozy.

Candidates and outside funding groups sometimes make legal yet sneaky moves in the final days before the election, leaving voters in the dark about who is funding their efforts.

That’s because any activity on or after Oct. 15 will not be made public until after Election Day. A lot of money from shadowy nonprofit groups, which do not disclose their donors, tends to flow into super PACs at the very end of the midterms.

Meantime, what the latest reports show is a trend that has been a defining factor in this year’s midterm races: Democratic candidates have out-raised Republican contenders in competitive races, but Republican groups have outpaced their Democratic counterparts.

The jump in oil prices has pushed up energy costs for Americans; gas now averages $4.29 a gallon, according to AAA.

A leaked advertisement in the Ohio governor’s race dominated the political conversation for much of last week. The explosive spot featured the estranged mother of Dr. Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor, calling her daughter a liar. Dr. Acton has said she has not spoken to her mother since she was 12 years old, when she was removed from her custody after her stepfather was arrested and charged with raping her.

Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate who has been trailing Dr. Acton in polls and whose campaign produced the spot, defended the ad — and bought $4 million in airtime to broadcast it — even as some Republicans denounced it. Then, over the weekend, his campaign replaced the original version, which was 60 seconds long, with a 30-second cut that excludes a mention of Dr. Acton’s childhood.

The ad has tested the boundaries of campaign attacks in the era of Trump politics. Neither party knows exactly whether the backlash could hurt Senator Jon Husted, the Republican incumbent trying to defend his seat in a tossup race. Mr. Husted said he would not have run the ad.

49 percent.

Polls have shown a tightening race in Maine in the final campaign stretch.

The cavalry has arrived in Florida, a state that remains a long shot for Democrats but where the races for Senate and especially for governor have been closer than expected.

Mr. Trump held a rally in the state last week and scheduled another one for this week to support Senator Ashley Moody, who is seeking election after she was appointed to replace Marco Rubio, and Representative Byron Donalds, who is running for governor. Over the weekend, former President Barack Obama, who won Florida twice, endorsed the Democratic candidates in both races, State Representative Angie Nixon for Senate and David Jolly for governor.

Last week, Mr. Jolly welcomed former President Bill Clinton to Hollywood, Fla., in what was Mr. Clinton’s first campaign trail appearance this election cycle. Mr. Clinton urged voters to elect “somebody who will wake up every morning thinking about what you need — not what will make President Trump happy.”

“He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened up a Cheesecake Factory.”

item.title: Data Center Industry Pushes for Darline Graham in South Carolina Senate Race
item.description:
In a preview of political fights to come over artificial intelligence, the data center industry is starting to spend money on elections for the first time.

The industry faces growing resistance. Data centers have become a symbol of voters’ anxiety over the rapid development of A.I., and polling shows that wide numbers of Americans are uncomfortable with their construction.

Now, the industry is pushing to assert its power. Its first goal: electing Senator Darline Graham, a Republican, to a full term in South Carolina, where she is in an unexpectedly tight race against Dr. Annie Andrews, a Democrat.

This month, a new super PAC aligned with the data center industry has reserved $1.5 million worth of advertising to help Ms. Graham. The spending is most likely the tip of the iceberg for the super PAC, Building the Future, which is aiming to exert more influence in the 2028 election cycle and beyond.

“Candidates who make the case that A.I. infrastructure investment will bring good-paying jobs, economic opportunity, and new revenue to local communities, while putting responsible protections in place and earning local support, will win races,” said Jesse Hunt, a spokesman for the group. “Building the Future will be there to help tell that story.”

The data center industry has reason to defend Ms. Graham, a first-time politician who was appointed after her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, died this summer. Her seat was considered safely Republican until polling showed Democrats gaining strength across the country, and a bitter special Republican primary election this summer left some Republican voters skeptical of Ms. Graham’s credentials.

Dr. Andrews has fiercely opposed data center developments. She has called for a two-year moratorium on new projects and nicknamed Ms. Graham “Data Center Darline.”

Ms. Graham has been friendlier toward the industry. She has tried to walk a line between framing data center development as a national security priority in a technological race against China, while stressing the need for community involvement. She has opposed moratoriums, arguing that halting construction would give China a dangerous advantage in artificial intelligence. She has also expressed support for local control over such projects.

“Sen. Graham trusts the people of South Carolina more than Washington politicians and believes America will beat China in any technological race,” T.W. Arrighi, a spokesman for Ms. Graham, said in a statement.

To help Ms. Graham, the data center super PAC has started airing two ads on her behalf. Neither of them mentions data centers, instead highlighting her work as commissioner of a state agency for blind residents.

Ms. Graham has lagged far behind Dr. Andrews in fund-raising. Since beginning to run ads on Oct. 17, Building the Future has been the second largest pro-Graham advertiser in the state, according to the media-tracking firm AdImpact.

Building the Future was created by the people who run a super PAC that supports the A.I. industry called Leading the Future. That group has spent tens of millions on pro-A.I. candidates. But after months in which candidates have attacked data centers specifically, the political operatives behind Leading the Future wanted an advocacy organization more narrowly focused on supporting candidates who vocally favor data centers. Building the Future has not yet disclosed any of its donors.

The super PAC was announced less than two weeks after the National Republican Senatorial Committee practically begged the data center industry to come to the defense of Republicans in the midterms. In a remarkable memo, the committee singled out Senator Jon Husted, a Republican facing a close race in Ohio, saying that data centers had “become a sleeper issue” and that the “toxic” data center industry “will be blamed” if he loses.

Two weeks after that memo, a nonprofit group tied to Building the Future, Build American AI, began a roughly $7 million ad campaign promoting the data center industry, primarily in Ohio and two other states where the issue threatens to be an anvil for Republicans, Kansas and Wisconsin

Last month, two other A.I.-linked nonprofit groups, the Meta-funded American Edge Project and a new group backed by four data center developers, Infrastructure for America, started spending on advertising to defend the industry.

Already, South Carolina has offered a preview of voters’ views of data centers.

Glenda Brady, 68, lives in Spartanburg County, a community with a huge data center under construction.

“They’re here to stay, and frankly, we need them,” said Ms. Brady, who is a volunteer with the county Republican Party. “We don’t need for China to have them, that’s for sure.”

But Pamela Miller, 55, who identifies as a “hard-core Republican,” said she would vote for Dr. Andrews next week in part because of Ms. Graham’s stance on data centers. She said she would not vote for a Republican “if they back data centers.”

At a rally last week at a livestock facility about an hour from the construction site of a new data center, President Trump said data centers would be “so popular” if nearby residents received paychecks for the inconvenience.

It was one of the few moments in an otherwise energetic rally that the crowd went quiet.

item.title: What to Know About Trump’s Rally in Mississippi
item.description:
President Trump’s tour of Republican strongholds this fall takes him on Monday to an unexpected battleground: Mississippi. There, he will campaign for Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican defending her seat in a race that has tightened over the last few months amid a barrage of late spending and visits from prominent Democrats.

Ms. Hyde-Smith, who has held the seat since 2018, is still favored to win. But her challenger, Scott Colom, a Democratic district attorney focused on improving health care access, lowering inflation and fighting corruption, has narrowed her lead, polls show. He is backed by a coalition of working-class Black and white voters.

Here’s what to know about the Senate race.

A Democrat has not won a Senate seat in Mississippi since 1982, and Mr. Trump won the state by about 23 points in 2024. The race still tilts toward Republicans, but the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, shifted its rating last week to “likely Republican” from “solid Republican.”

Democrats face a steep challenge to regain control of the Senate — they must flip four Republican-held seats, including some in states Mr. Trump won by double digits — but have put Republicans on defense even in deep-red areas of the country.

Super PACs connected to both parties have invested in the Senate contest, and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned for Mr. Colom in Mississippi last week.

Mr. Colom also recently went viral for a 30-second campaign ad mocking Ms. Hyde-Smith’s tone-deaf response to a local television anchor’s comment on the rising price of beef: “You have so many proteins to choose from,” she says in a clip.

The video cuts to a man grilling. “Pick another protein?” he says. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

Mr. Colom, a district attorney, has used charisma and charm on the trail to turn a difficult seat for Democrats into a potential target. High-profile Democrats like Ms. Harris and Senators Cory Booker of New Jersey and Raphael Warnock of Georgia have campaigned with him, and former President Barack Obama filmed an endorsement ad for him.

If he wins, Mr. Colom would be Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. Though he has played down that potential milestone, he has appealed to Mississippi’s Black community, a crucial group that counts for about 37 percent of all residents, the largest share of any state.

Mr. Colom cast Mr. Trump’s visit as a sign of concerns that Ms. Hyde-Smith might lose.

“Cindy High Prices is scared and that’s why she’s sending Donald Trump down here,” Mr. Colom wrote on social media last week. “She’s scared to answer why she voted to cut healthcare, why she betrayed our farmers and why she blocked the release of the Epstein files.”

Mr. Trump, asked last week how worried he was about Ms. Hyde-Smith’s chances, told reporters that she was “very popular” and that he had won the state “in a landslide.” He said: “If I need to get her over the top, I would go there.”

On Friday, he told reporters that he was traveling to Mississippi because he had been asked to go. “She’s up in the polls,” he said. “She’s not losing.”

Jake Monssen, Ms. Hyde-Smith’s campaign manager, said on Monday that “Mississippians aren’t too keen” on Mr. Colom because of his liberal policies. “I think we’re in a good spot,” he added.

item.title: Is the Venice Soccer Team Ever Going to Be as Good as It Looks?
item.description:
Dressed in sleek black jerseys in their picturesque stadium perched on a lagoon, the Venice soccer team was taking a beating.

A defender slipped on the turf, and the opposing team, from Florence, scored an easy goal. A Venice striker sent a kick soaring so high over the crossbar that it seemed aimed at the Adriatic Sea. The team’s captain was forced off with an ankle injury.

When Florence went 4-1 ahead in the game last month, some supporters left the stadium early. “Change the defense, change everything!” Ettore Saramin, 75, shouted. “They are humiliating us!”

Venezia FC lost 4-2.

But as the mood sank at the floating stadium, off the pitch the hype around the club kept soaring.

On Instagram, the team’s promotional rollouts are a gallery of gritty Italian glam. Their kit has become a cult style hit. All sorts of influencers, models and celebrities — the Libertines singer Pete Doherty, the bass player Victoria De Angelis from the Italian rock band Maneskin, the British artist Corbin Shaw — have worn the Venezia FC jersey, turning a provincial soccer team into a fashion sensation.

“It’s really becoming a cool thing,” said Guilherme Torres, who works in an art gallery in São Paulo and was wearing a team jersey at an art fair in Buenos Aires last month.

Fueling this rise is a branding push backed by the team’s American owners that is aimed at propelling Venezia FC past its modest local audience and volatile soccer standing. The effort was rewarded in the last soccer season when the team was promoted to Serie A, Italy’s top league.

But after six straight losses to start the season, the team occupies last place in Serie A, raising the possibility that it could be demoted and one pressing question: Is the Venice soccer team ever going to be as good as it looks?

On a recent evening, aboard a water bus heading to the Venice stadium, a supporter had thoughts.

“It is no use,” said Oliviero Cassará, 44, “to have cool T-shirts if your team sucks.”

The Venice soccer team was founded in 1907 and has played for more than a century at the Pier Luigi Penzo stadium, which is perched on the shore of the Venetian Island of Sant’Elena. Games are frequented by locals who show equal commitment to watching the soccer and to knocking back Aperol Spritzes in the surrounding taverns. Since the 1950s, the team has made only one- or two-year stints in Serie A, tacking back and forth through Italian leagues and financial turmoil.

In 2020, a former chief executive of the New York Stock Exchange, Duncan Niederauer, became the club’s primary owner and president, and the whole club got a thorough polish.

“It got a very stylish and fashionable cut,” said the club’s chief revenue officer, Nicola Boscaro, an effort to link the team “as closely as possible to the city of Venice.”

The German design studio Bureau Borsche was hired to redesign the team’s visual identity. It replaced the traditional crest with a geometric, slightly midcentury modern golden V. Soccer players posing awkwardly in knee-high socks were out; the Greek model Theopisti Pourliotopoulou, lounging on a gondola, was in.

Leaving behind a sartorial tradition of pedestrian sportswear, the team adopted vintage-looking gold and black pieces, all photographed in saturated, fashionable light against the backdrop of Venice’s lagoon.

The Bureau Borsche’s aesthetic did not merely glorify Venice’s ancient past; it also reflected the hip allure that Venice reflects during the opening week of its Biennale, when flocks of Europeans wearing Japanese cotton pants animate the old, and sometimes melancholic, city with fresh talent, a contemporary edge and an infinite supply of canvas bags.

The designers hired trendy French models like Solange Smith, but also Venetian artists like Fabrizio Plessi to pose for the brand, embracing an aesthetic of decadent Italian chic that has spread widely on Instagram.

The team’s Instagram posts feature older Italian women standing on a balcony wrapped in Venice flags, as well as kitschy foulards, gondoliers wearing a blazing red Venice soccer jersey and cinematographic drone footage of Venice. A partnership between Nike and the rapper Drake, NOCTA, designed the most recent collections.

“I really like the colors and the design,” said Shirley Garrier, a French food influencer who wore the Venice jersey in a cooking video.

Many soccer clubs are reinventing themselves as fashion brands to drive revenue, but Venezia FC was different because it was not a famous club. Until it decided to leverage its city’s international prestige.

“Nobody knew that there was a soccer team in Venice,” said Mirko Borsche of the German studio. “But everyone knew Venice.”

The club has also focused on improving the team’s performance. This year, it secured the most expensive signing in its history, the Nigerian striker Akor Adams, for over 16 million euros, about $18 million.

But executives said the team’s success could exist independently of soccer goals. While scoring in games “definitely helps,” said Mr. Boscaro, the revenue officer, “the current model is not built around winning.”

“Victories are more relevant for the Venetian supporter,” he added. They really are.

After the Florence game, Venetian fans nervously clutched their Spritz glasses at the local Vincent Bar.

“It was tough,” said Stefano Lo chiatto, 35.

The whole season has been tough. Venice has so far won only one game, against Naples, and has lost against AC Milan, Lecce, Frosinone, Lazio, Atalanta and Genoa, as well as Florence. On Oct. 13, the team announced that its coach would be changed.

Fans are excited about the club’s new fashionable allure, but in the first days of the rebranding some were sorry that the original colors of orange, green and black were in some jerseys changed to golden, or white and burgundy. They have been changed back in this year’s edition.

Many supporters also resent the club’s project to build a new, much larger stadium on the mainland that would be reachable by car. In a city that in recent years had lost many of its residents, and most services catering to them, losing the stadium seemed like a betrayal.

“The butcher, the baker, there is nothing left anymore,” said Matteo Crivellaro, 33. “With the stadium on the mainland you are taking away another piece of identity from Venice and selling it out to tourists.”

The Venice stadium differs from many contemporary commercial soccer arenas. It is relatively small, holding just 10,000 people, and it is reachable only after a long water bus journey.

But to supporters, the ritual of wearing comfortable shoes and walking Venice’s flagstones under the heavy November humidity or the blistering summer heat to watch their team play on the water was what Ultimo Uomo, an Italian soccer magazine, has called “one of the world’s most beautiful walks.”

Mr. Boscaro, the revenue officer, conceded that the Pier Luigi Penzo stadium was “very romantic,” but he said that the new one was critical to broadening the audience, increasing revenue and attracting better players.

A new audience has already started showing up around the stadium; they are influencers who, said Diego Carraro, 50, a longtime Venice supporter, “burn through two phone batteries” taking photos during games.

But die-hard supporters doubt the staying power of the influencer crowd.

“When it rains,” Mr. Crivellaro said, “they will go away.”
